To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we computationally identified synthetic carbon fixation pathways that are faster than the natural ones.
we computationally identified novel synthetic carbon fixation pathways that could be more efficient than their natural counterparts.

we computationally identified novel carbon fixation pathways that are predicted to be more efficient than the Calvin-Benson cycle, and that one such pathway employs the most effective known carboxylating enzymes, phosphoenol pyruvate carboylase, using a core of the naturally-evolved C4 cycle.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and analysis of alternative carbon fixation pathways using the entire metabolic repertoire of approximately 5000 enzymes.
the design of synthetic metabolic pathways.
the design and analysis of synthetic pathways for carbon fixation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the proposed synthetic carbon fixation cycles have significant advantages in comparison to the natural counterparts, which could lead to a substantial increase in the rate of carbon fixation and, consequently, to increased biomass production.

the proposed synthetic carbon fixation pathways could provide a significant quantitative advantage over the natural counterparts, and that the most efficient synthetic pathway identified is predicted to be 2–3 times faster than the C4 cycle.
there is no reason to think that the synthetic pathways we have identified would be more effective than the natural pathways.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are proposing a new approach for engineering metabolic pathways, in which we use the entire metabolic repertoire of nature as the building blocks for the design of novel synthetic metabolic pathways.
the design of synthetic metabolic pathways can be a promising strategy for improving the efficiency of biological carbon fixation, which is a critical bottleneck for sustainable agriculture.
we have designed synthetic carbon fixation cycles that are predicted to be more efficient than the Calvin– Benson cycle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
nature has not found the best possible way to perform a given function.
it is possible to identify synthetic metabolic cycles, which are predicted to be superior to natural cycles in terms of kinetics and topology.

the metabolic repertoire of the living organisms on the planet is so rich that it allows the construction of alternative pathways that could have significant quantitative and qualitative advantages over their natural predecessors.
